trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly calculating coordinate points for one or both equations.
Inaccurate plotting of points on the graph.
Inaccurate plotting of points on the graph.
Failing to identify the intersection point correctly or misinterpreting parallel/coincident lines.

nodes.name: Solve Word Problem using Graphical Method
method_steps: Identify the two unknown quantities in the word problem and assign variables (e.g., x and y) to them.
Translate the conditions given in the word problem into two linear equations in terms of the assigned variables.
For each equation, select at least two x-values (or y-values) and calculate the corresponding y-values (or x-values) to find two coordinate points.
Plot the calculated coordinate points for the first equation on a Cartesian plane.
Draw a straight line passing through these points for the first equation.
Plot the calculated coordinate points for the second equation on the same Cartesian plane.
Draw a straight line passing through these points for the second equation.
Identify the intersection point of the two lines, if it exists.
State the coordinates of the intersection point as the solution (x, y) and interpret them back into the context of the word problem.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly forming one or both linear equations from the word problem.
Incorrectly calculating coordinate points for one or both equations.
Inaccurate plotting of points on the graph.
Inaccurate plotting of points on the graph.
Failing to identify the intersection point correctly or misinterpreting parallel/coincident lines.
Failing to interpret the numerical solution back into the context of the word problem.

nodes.name: Classifying Systems of Linear Equations by Coefficient Ratios
method_steps: Write the two linear equations in standard form: a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0.
Calculate the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, and c₁/c₂.
Compare a₁/a₂ and b₁/b₂.
If a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, the lines intersect at a unique point; the system is consistent and has a unique solution.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂, then compare this ratio with c₁/c₂.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel and never intersect; the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂, the lines are coincident (overlap); the system is dependent (and consistent) and has infinitely many solutions.

trap_steps.trap: Assuming all systems must have a unique solution regardless of ratios.
Confusing conditions for parallel lines with coincident lines (inconsistent vs. dependent).
Confusing conditions for coincident lines with parallel lines (dependent vs. inconsistent).

nodes.name: Solving Systems of Linear Equations Algebraically (Substitution/Elimination)
method_steps: Identify the unknown quantities and define variables for them (e.g., 'x' and 'y').
Translate the problem's conditions into two linear equations in terms of the defined variables.
Solve the system of equations using either the substitution method or the elimination method.
If a unique solution for both variables is found, the system is consistent and has a unique solution.
If an identity (e.g., 0 = 0 or 18 = 18) is obtained, the system is dependent (and consistent) and has infinitely many solutions.
If a contradiction (e.g., 0 = 5 or -4 = 0) is obtained, the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
State the answer in the context of the original problem (for word problems).

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the linear equations from the word problem description.
Assuming all systems must have a unique solution and forcing one when an identity or contradiction occurs.
Misinterpreting an identity (e.g., 0=0) as 'no solution' or a calculation error.
Misinterpreting a contradiction (e.g., 0=5) as a solvable system or a calculation error leading to a unique solution.

nodes.name: Graphical Method for Solving and Classifying Systems of Linear Equations
method_steps: Rewrite each linear equation into a form suitable for graphing (e.g., slope-intercept form y = mx + c, or standard form Ax + By = C to find intercepts).
For each equation, find at least two points that satisfy it (e.g., x-intercept and y-intercept).
Plot these points on a coordinate plane and draw a straight line through them for each equation.
Observe the relationship between the two drawn lines.
If the lines intersect at a single point, the system is consistent, has a unique solution, and the coordinates of the intersection point are the solution.
If the lines are parallel (never intersect), the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
If the lines are coincident (overlap completely), the system is dependent (and consistent) and has infinitely many solutions.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly calculating points for plotting due to arithmetic errors or sign mistakes.
Drawing inaccurate lines on the graph, leading to incorrect intersection points or misidentification of parallel/coincident lines.
Misinterpreting parallel lines as intersecting, or coincident lines as parallel.

nodes.name: Classify System of Equations by Coefficient Ratios
method_steps: Write the given linear equations in standard form (a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0).
Identify the coefficients a1, b1, c1, a2, b2, c2.
Calculate the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2, and c1/c2.

Compare the ratios: If a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2 (unique solution, intersecting lines); If a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2 (no solution, parallel lines); If a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 (infinitely many solutions, coincident lines).
State the type of solution and corresponding graphical representation based on the comparison.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying coefficients, especially signs or zero coefficients.
Calculation errors when forming ratios or swapping terms.
Misinterpreting ratio comparison results (e.g., confusing parallel with coincident lines).

nodes.name: Determine System Consistency and Solve Graphically
method_steps: Write the given linear equations in standard form (a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0).
Identify the coefficients a1, b1, c1, a2, b2, c2.
Calculate the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2, and c1/c2.
Compare the ratios to determine consistency: If a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2 or a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, the system is consistent. If a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2, the system is inconsistent.
If the system is consistent, find at least two solutions (x, y pairs) for each equation to prepare for graphing.
Plot these points and draw the lines representing each equation on a graph.
Identify the point of intersection (for unique solution) or observe coincident lines (for infinite solutions) and state the solution(s).

trap_steps.trap: Calculation errors when forming ratios or swapping terms.
Misinterpreting ratio comparison results for consistency.
Errors in calculating points for graphing, leading to incorrect line plots.
Inaccurate plotting or misreading the intersection point from the graph.

nodes.name: Word Problem: Formulate Equations, then Graphically Solve/Analyze
method_steps: Read the word problem carefully to understand the context and identify unknown quantities.
Define variables (e.g., x, y) to represent the unknown quantities.
Translate the conditions given in the word problem into a pair of linear equations.
Write the equations in standard form (a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0) if not already.
Calculate and compare coefficient ratios (a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2) to predict the nature of solutions (unique, no, infinite) or consistency (optional, depending on the question).
Find at least two solutions (x, y pairs) for each equation to prepare for graphing.
Plot these points and draw the lines representing each equation on a graph.
Interpret the graphical solution in the context of the word problem (e.g., find specific values, or state whether a condition is met).

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating verbal statements into algebraic equations, leading to an incorrect system of equations.
Errors in calculating ratios or misinterpreting results.
Calculation errors when finding points for graphing.
Failing to relate the mathematical solution (e.g., intersection point) back to the specific question asked in the word problem.

nodes.name: Solving a system of linear equations using the substitution method (given equations)
method_steps: Choose one equation and isolate one variable in terms of the other (e.g., solve for x in terms of y).
Substitute the expression for the isolated variable into the *other* equation.
Solve the resulting single-variable linear equation for that variable.
Substitute the value found in the previous step back into the expression from the first step to find the value of the second variable.
State the solution as an ordered pair (x, y) or as individual variable values.

trap_steps.trap: Algebraic errors (e.g., sign errors, division errors) when isolating a variable.
Incorrectly substituting the expression into the same equation, or making algebraic errors during the substitution process.

Algebraic errors when solving the single-variable linear equation, or misinterpreting cases of no solution (e.g., ending with a false statement like -4=0) or infinite solutions (e.g., ending with a true statement like 0=0).
Algebraic errors during back-substitution to find the second variable.

nodes.name: Solving word problems by formulating linear equations and using the substitution method
method_steps: Identify the unknown quantities in the word problem and assign variables (e.g., x, y) to represent them.
Translate the problem's conditions and relationships into a system of two linear equations in terms of the assigned variables.
Choose one equation and isolate one variable in terms of the other.
Substitute the expression for the isolated variable into the *other* equation.
Solve the resulting single-variable linear equation for that variable.
Substitute the value found in the previous step back into the expression from step 3 to find the value of the second variable.
State the final answer clearly in the context of the original word problem.
isomorphic_variables: specific quantities (ages, distances, costs, number of items)
context (age problem, money problem, fraction problem, etc.)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying the unknown quantities or assigning variables that do not clearly represent them.

Incorrectly setting up the equations from the word problem, misinterpreting relationships (e.g., 'seven times as old' vs. 'seven years older'), or formulating equations that do not accurately reflect the problem's conditions.
Algebraic errors when isolating a variable from one of the formulated equations.
Incorrectly substituting the expression into the second equation, or making algebraic errors during the substitution.
Algebraic errors when solving the single-variable linear equation.
Algebraic errors during back-substitution to find the second variable.
Not stating the answer in the context of the word problem, or misinterpreting the calculated values in relation to the original question.

nodes.name: Solving System of Linear Equations using Elimination Method
method_steps: Ensure both equations are in the standard form (Ax + By = C).
Choose one variable to eliminate.
Multiply one or both equations by suitable non-zero constants to make the absolute values of the coefficients of the chosen variable equal.
Add or subtract the modified equations to eliminate the chosen variable.
Solve the resulting linear equation in one variable.
Substitute the value obtained into either of the original equations.
Solve for the second variable.
isomorphic_variables: equations (different forms reducible to standard form)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly multiplying an equation by a constant, forgetting to multiply all terms (including the constant term on the right side).
Algebraic errors during addition or subtraction of equations, especially with negative signs, leading to incorrect elimination or combining terms.
Mistakes in solving the resulting single-variable equation (e.g., division errors, sign errors).

nodes.name: Age Word Problems Solved by Elimination Method
method_steps: Identify the unknown present ages and assign variables, then formulate two linear equations from the problem conditions.
Multiply one or both equations by non-zero constants to make the absolute values of the coefficients of one variable equal.
Add or subtract the modified equations to eliminate one variable.
Solve the resulting linear equation in one variable.
Substitute the found value into an original equation and solve for the other variable.
State the present ages of all individuals.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating 'years hence' or 'years ago' into algebraic expressions (e.g., forgetting to add/subtract from both sides of the age relation).
Incorrectly multiplying an equation by a constant, forgetting to multiply all terms.
Algebraic errors during addition or subtraction of equations, especially with negative signs.

nodes.name: Two-Digit Number Word Problems Solved by Elimination Method
method_steps: Define variables for the digits (e.g., ten's digit as x, unit's digit as y) and express the original and reversed numbers algebraically (10x+y, 10y+x).
Formulate two linear equations from the problem conditions based on the relationships between digits and numbers.
Multiply one or both equations by non-zero constants to make the absolute values of the coefficients of one variable equal.
Add or subtract the modified equations to eliminate one variable.
Solve the resulting linear equation in one variable for its value.
Substitute the value obtained into one of the original equations and solve for the other digit.
Form the final two-digit number using the found digits.
isomorphic_variables: relationships involving the number and its reversed form

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly representing the two-digit number (e.g., writing x + y instead of 10x + y) or the reversed number.
Errors in translating the word problem's conditions into correct algebraic equations.
Incorrectly multiplying an equation by a constant, forgetting to multiply all terms.
Algebraic errors during addition or subtraction of equations, especially with negative signs.

nodes.name: Formulate quadratic equation from word problem
method_steps: Read and understand the word problem to identify unknown quantities.
Assign variables (e.g., 'x') to the unknown quantities.
Translate the given conditions and relationships into algebraic expressions and equations.
Combine expressions to form a single equation based on the problem's criteria.
Simplify the equation by expanding products, collecting like terms, and moving all terms to one side.
Check if the simplified equation is in the standard form `ax^2 + bx + c = 0` where `a ≠ 0`.
isomorphic_variables: context: marbles, toys, area, speed, age

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating verbal relationships into algebraic expressions (e.g., 'product' vs 'sum').
Algebraic errors during expansion or simplification, leading to incorrect powers of x or incorrect coefficients.
Failing to check if the leading coefficient (a) is zero after simplification, or confusing the resulting equation with a linear or cubic one.
Not understanding that for an equation to be quadratic, the coefficient of x^2 (a) cannot be zero.

nodes.name: Check if a given algebraic equation is quadratic
method_steps: Simplify both sides of the given equation by expanding any products or powers.
Combine like terms on each side.
Move all terms to one side of the equation, setting the other side to zero.
Combine any remaining like terms to obtain the simplest form `Ax^n + Bx^(n-1) + ... = 0`.
Identify the highest power of the variable (`x`) in the simplified equation.
If the highest power is 2 and the coefficient of the `x^2` term is non-zero, then it is a quadratic equation; otherwise, it is not.
isomorphic_variables: form of initial equation (e.g., product of binomials, squared terms, cubic terms)

trap_steps.trap: Algebraic errors when expanding expressions (e.g., (x+a)^2 = x^2+a^2 instead of x^2+2ax+a^2, or distributive property errors).
Sign errors when moving terms from one side of the equation to the other.
Failing to correctly combine all like terms.
Incorrectly identifying the highest power of the variable after simplification, especially if terms cancel out.
Assuming an equation is quadratic if it *initially* contains an x^2 term, without simplifying to check if it cancels out.
Forgetting that the coefficient 'a' of the x^2 term must not be zero for it to be a quadratic equation.
Confusing a quadratic equation with a linear equation (if x^2 terms cancel) or a cubic equation (if x^3 terms remain).

nodes.name: Formulating Quadratic Equations from Word Problems
method_steps: Read and understand the problem statement to identify unknown quantities and relationships.
Assign a variable (e.g., 'x') to one of the unknown quantities.
Express other unknown quantities or relationships in terms of the chosen variable 'x'.
Translate the given conditions and relationships into a single algebraic equation.
Simplify the algebraic equation by expanding, combining like terms, and moving all terms to one side, setting the other side to zero.
Write the equation in the standard form 'ax^2 + bx + c = 0'.
Verify that the coefficient 'a' of the 'x^2' term is non-zero to confirm it is a quadratic equation.
isomorphic_variables: numeric values in the problem description

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating the word problem's conditions into an algebraic equation.
Errors in expanding expressions or combining like terms during simplification.
Failing to check if the coefficient 'a' of the x^2 term is non-zero, or misidentifying the highest power after simplification.

nodes.name: Identifying Quadratic Equations by Algebraic Simplification
method_steps: Clear any parentheses, distribute terms, and expand all algebraic expressions on both sides of the equation.
Move all terms to one side of the equation, setting the other side to zero.
Combine all like terms.
Write the simplified equation in the standard form 'ax^2 + bx + c = 0'.
Identify the highest power of the variable (degree) in the simplified equation.
If the highest power is 2 and the coefficient 'a' (of the 'x^2' term) is non-zero, then the given equation is a quadratic equation; otherwise, it is not.

trap_steps.trap: Errors in expanding algebraic identities (e.g., (a+b)^2, (a-b)^3) or distributing terms incorrectly.
Errors in combining like terms, especially with signs.
Incorrectly identifying the highest power of the variable after simplification, especially if terms cancel out.
Failing to verify that the coefficient 'a' of the x^2 term is non-zero after simplification.

nodes.name: Forming Quadratic Equations from Quantity-Based Word Problems with Modifications
method_steps: Identify the unknown quantities and any known total or initial relationship between them from the problem statement.
Assign a single variable (e.g., 'x') to one of the primary unknown quantities.
Express all other unknown quantities or dimensions in terms of the chosen variable 'x' and any given constants.
Identify any subsequent modifications (e.g., 'lost', 'gained', 'increased by', 'decreased by') applied to these quantities.
Write algebraic expressions for the quantities *after* these modifications have been applied.
Identify the final condition or relationship (e.g., product, area, new total, difference) that connects the modified quantities.
Formulate an algebraic equation by setting up the relationship from step 6 using the expressions from step 5.
Simplify and rearrange the equation into the standard quadratic form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
isomorphic_variables: names_of_entities (e.g., John, Jivanti; length, width; speed of A, speed of B)
type_of_quantity (e.g., marbles, age, side length, number of items)
final_relationship_type (e.g., product, sum, area, new difference)
context (e.g., marbles game, money distribution, geometric shapes)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly expressing a dependent quantity in terms of 'x' (e.g., adding instead of subtracting from a total, or misinterpreting the relationship).
Failing to apply modifications correctly to all affected quantities or misinterpreting the direction of change (e.g., x+5 instead of x-5 for 'lost 5').
Setting up the main equation incorrectly based on the final relationship (e.g., confusing product with sum, or using initial quantities instead of the modified ones).
Making algebraic errors during simplification and rearrangement, leading to an incorrect quadratic form or failing to achieve the standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.

nodes.name: Formulate Quadratic Equation from Word Problem
method_steps: Read the problem carefully and identify the unknown quantities.
Assign a variable (e.g., 'x') to one of the unknown quantities.
Express other unknown quantities in terms of the chosen variable.
Translate the given relationships or conditions into an algebraic equation.
Simplify and rearrange the equation to the standard quadratic form ax² + bx + c = 0.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly relating variables (e.g., age difference vs. product, consecutive integers setup).
Incorrectly translating verbal relationships into mathematical operations (e.g., 'product is' becoming addition).
Algebraic errors when simplifying or rearranging to the standard form.

nodes.name: Identify if an Equation is Quadratic
method_steps: Simplify both sides of the given equation by expanding products and combining like terms.
Move all terms to one side of the equation, setting the other side to zero.
Combine any remaining like terms.
Examine the resulting equation to see if it is in the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, where 'a' is not equal to zero.

trap_steps.trap: Algebraic errors during expansion (e.g., (x-2)² ≠ x²-4).
Errors in combining like terms or moving terms across the equality sign (sign changes).
Incorrectly concluding if 'a' is zero or not, or if the highest power is not 2 (e.g., x² + x = x² + 5 is simplified to x=5, not quadratic).

nodes.name: Find Roots by Factorization
method_steps: Ensure the quadratic equation is in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Find two numbers whose product is (a * c) and whose sum is (b).
Rewrite the middle term 'bx' using these two numbers (splitting the middle term).
Factor by grouping the terms.
Set each linear factor equal to zero and solve for the variable 'x'.

trap_steps.trap: Difficulty finding the correct pair of numbers for the product 'ac' and sum 'b'.
Algebraic errors when rewriting the middle term 'bx'.
Errors in grouping terms or factoring out common factors.
Algebraic errors when solving the resulting linear equations from the factors.

nodes.name: Analyze and Find Roots using Discriminant and Quadratic Formula
method_steps: Ensure the quadratic equation is in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Identify the coefficients a, b, and c.
Calculate the discriminant, D = b² - 4ac.
Determine the nature of the roots based on the discriminant (D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: two equal real roots; D < 0: no real roots).
If real roots exist (D ≥ 0), apply the quadratic formula: x = (-b ± √(D)) / (2a) to find the roots.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying coefficients a, b, or c, especially with negative signs or missing terms (e.g., if b=0).
Calculation errors for b² - 4ac, particularly with negative numbers (e.g., (-4)² vs -4²).
Incorrectly interpreting the discriminant (e.g., thinking D < 0 means one real root).
Algebraic errors when applying the quadratic formula, especially with negative 'b', the '±' sign, or division by '2a'.

nodes.name: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorization (Standard Form)
method_steps: Rewrite the quadratic equation in standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Identify coefficients a, b, and c.
Find two integers p and q such that p + q = b and p * q = a * c.
Rewrite the middle term bx as px + qx.
Group the terms and factor out common monomials to obtain two linear factors (Dx + E)(Fx + G).
Set each linear factor equal to zero: Dx + E = 0 and Fx + G = 0.
Solve each linear equation for x to find the two roots.
(Optional) Verify the roots by substituting them back into the original equation.
isomorphic_variables: numerical values of coefficients (a, b, c)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying two numbers p and q for splitting the middle term, or struggling to find such numbers.
Errors in factoring by grouping or extracting common factors.
Failing to set *each* linear factor to zero, or incorrectly assuming only one factor yields a solution.

nodes.name: Word Problems Leading to Quadratic Equations (Factorization Method)
method_steps: Read the problem carefully to understand the context and identify the unknown quantities.
Assign a variable (e.g., x) to one of the unknown quantities.
Express all other relevant unknown quantities in terms of the chosen variable.
Translate the given conditions and relationships in the word problem into a mathematical equation.
Simplify the equation and rewrite it in the standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Solve the quadratic equation using the factorization method (by splitting the middle term, grouping, and setting each linear factor to zero to find potential roots).
Evaluate each potential root in the context of the original word problem and discard any solutions that are not physically or logically possible (e.g., negative length, fractional number of people).
State the final answer(s) clearly with units if applicable.
isomorphic_variables: numerical values in the problem (e.g., ages, distances, product results)
context of the word problem (e.g., marbles, ages, train, prayer hall, consecutive integers)
specific relationships described (e.g., 'older than', 'product is', 'km/h less')

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating problem conditions into an algebraic equation, leading to an incorrect quadratic form.
Errors in simplifying the derived equation into standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Errors in applying the factorization method, such as mis-splitting the middle term or mistakes in grouping terms.
Failing to set each linear factor obtained from factorization to zero, leading to missing one or both roots.
Not checking the validity of roots in the problem's context or misinterpreting the physical meaning of solutions (e.g., accepting negative lengths or non-integer counts).

nodes.name: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorization
method_steps: Rewrite the quadratic equation in standard form `ax^2 + bx + c = 0`.
Identify coefficients `a`, `b`, and `c`.
Find two numbers (let's call them `p` and `q`) such that their product is `ac` and their sum is `b`.
Rewrite the middle term `bx` as `px + qx`.
Group the terms into two pairs and factor out the greatest common monomial from each pair.
Factor out the common binomial factor.
Set each linear factor equal to zero and solve for `x` to find the roots.

nodes.name: Determine Nature of Roots for a Given Quadratic Equation
method_steps: Identify the coefficients a, b, and c from the quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Calculate the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac.
Compare the value of D with 0.
If D > 0, conclude there are two distinct real roots.
If D = 0, conclude there are two equal real roots.
If D < 0, conclude there are no real roots.
If real roots exist and are requested, find them using the quadratic formula.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly calculating b^2 - 4ac due to sign errors, squaring negative numbers, or arithmetic mistakes.
Misinterpreting the sign of the discriminant (e.g., D < 0 means real roots, or D = 0 implies distinct roots).

nodes.name: Word Problem: Check Feasibility using Discriminant
method_steps: Translate the word problem into a mathematical model, leading to a quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Identify the coefficients a, b, and c from the quadratic equation.
Calculate the discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac.
Compare the value of D with 0.
If D < 0, conclude that no real solution exists for the problem, meaning the scenario is not possible or feasible.
If D >= 0, conclude that real solutions exist, meaning the scenario is possible or feasible.
If feasible and requested, find the real roots using the quadratic formula and interpret them in the context of the problem, discarding unrealistic solutions (e.g., negative length).

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly formulating the quadratic equation from the word problem, e.g., setting up the wrong relationship or making algebraic errors during translation.
Not understanding what 'no real roots' means in the context of the word problem (e.g., concluding it's possible even if D < 0).
Not interpreting the mathematical roots in the context of the problem (e.g., accepting negative length as a valid solution).

nodes.name: Find Unknown Coefficient for Specific Nature of Roots
method_steps: Ensure the given equation is in the standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Identify the coefficients a, b, and c, which will include the unknown coefficient (e.g., k).
Set up the discriminant equation based on the specified nature of roots (e.g., D = 0 for two equal real roots, D > 0 for two distinct real roots, D >= 0 for real roots).
Substitute the coefficients into the discriminant equation.
Solve the resulting equation (or inequality) for the unknown coefficient.
Verify the found value(s) in the original quadratic equation.
isomorphic_variables: position of unknown (in a, b, or c)
specific root condition (equal, real, distinct real, no real)

trap_steps.trap: Failing to expand or rearrange the equation into standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 before identifying coefficients.
Incorrectly applying the condition for the nature of roots (e.g., using D > 0 instead of D = 0 for equal roots, or vice versa).
Making algebraic errors when solving the resulting equation or inequality for the unknown coefficient.

nodes.name: Number, Age, or General Relationship Word Problems
method_steps: Identify unknown quantities and assign a variable (e.g., x) to one, expressing others in terms of x.
Formulate an algebraic equation based on the problem's conditions (e.g., product, sum of squares).
Rearrange the equation into the standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Solve the quadratic equation using an appropriate method (factorization, quadratic formula, etc.).
Check solutions for validity within the problem's context (e.g., positive integers, positive ages).
State the final answer(s) for all requested quantities.
isomorphic_variables: numerical relationships (e.g., consecutive, older/younger, multiple of)
specific numerical values (e.g., ages, product values, integer values, number of articles)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the initial equation from the word problem description, especially for relationships involving 'from now' or 'ago', or products/sums.
Failing to reject solutions that are physically impossible or don't make sense in the problem's context (e.g., negative age, fractional people when seeking integers).

nodes.name: Geometric Measurement Word Problems
method_steps: Draw a diagram (if helpful), identify unknown dimensions, and assign variables, expressing others in terms of one variable.
Formulate an equation based on geometric relationships (e.g., area, perimeter, Pythagorean theorem).
Rearrange the equation into the standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Solve the quadratic equation.
Check solutions for validity as physical dimensions (e.g., non-negative lengths).
State the final answer(s) for the requested dimensions.
isomorphic_variables: shape (e.g., rectangle, square, circular park, right triangle)
measurements (e.g., area, perimeter, diameter, distances, side lengths)
specific numerical values (e.g., dimensions, given values for area/perimeter/distance)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly applying geometric formulas or theorems to set up the equation (e.g., area formula, Pythagorean theorem, relationships in a circle).
Accepting negative or zero lengths/dimensions as valid solutions.

nodes.name: Speed, Distance, and Time Word Problems
method_steps: Identify different scenarios or parts of the journey and assign a variable (e.g., x for speed).
Express other quantities (e.g., time taken for each part) in terms of the variable, using the relationship 'Time = Distance / Speed'.
Formulate an equation based on the given conditions (e.g., difference in times, total time, total distance).
Simplify the equation, often by clearing denominators, into the standard quadratic form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Solve the quadratic equation.
Check solutions for validity within the problem's context (e.g., speed or time cannot be negative or zero).
State the final answer(s) for the requested quantities.
isomorphic_variables: mode of transport (e.g., train, car, boat, plane)
changes in speed (e.g., increased/decreased by X km/h)
changes in time (e.g., took X hours more/less)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the equation, especially when dealing with differences in time or inverted fractions for speed/time, or missing units.
Accepting negative or zero speed/time as valid solutions.

nodes.name: Identify Arithmetic Progression and its Basic Properties
method_steps: List the terms of the given sequence: a1, a2, a3, ...
Calculate the difference between consecutive terms: d1 = a2 - a1, d2 = a3 - a2, etc.
Compare the calculated differences.
If all differences are constant, the sequence is an Arithmetic Progression. Otherwise, it is not.
If it is an AP, identify the first term 'a' (which is a1).
The common difference 'd' is the constant difference found in step 4.
If asked, generate subsequent terms by adding 'd' to the last known term.

trap_steps.trap: Subtracting terms in the wrong order (e.g., a1 - a2 instead of a2 - a1), leading to an incorrect common difference.
Concluding it's an AP after checking only one pair of terms, or incorrectly identifying an AP when it's another type of sequence (e.g., Geometric Progression).
Believing the common difference 'd' must always be positive.

nodes.name: Calculate nth Term or Missing Terms in an Arithmetic Progression
method_steps: Identify the first term 'a' and the common difference 'd' of the AP. If not directly given, calculate 'd' from consecutive terms.
Recall the formula for the nth term of an AP: an = a + (n - 1)d.
If finding a specific 'n'th term: Substitute 'a', 'd', and the term position 'n' into the formula to calculate an.
If finding the term position 'n' (given an, a, d): Substitute known values into the formula and solve the linear equation for 'n'.
If 'n' is found, verify it is a positive integer. If not, the given an is not a term of the AP.

If finding missing terms within a sequence: Use the formula an = a + (n - 1)d or work iteratively by adding/subtracting 'd' to/from known terms. If two non-consecutive terms ak and am are known, find 'd' using the relation am - ak = (m - k)d.

trap_steps.trap: Error in calculating common difference 'd', especially with negative numbers or fractions.
Using an incorrect formula, e.g., an = a + nd instead of an = a + (n-1)d.
Failing to check if the calculated 'n' is a positive integer, implying a non-existent term or position.
Incorrectly calculating 'd' when finding missing terms between non-consecutive known terms.

nodes.name: Solve for AP Parameters (a, d) from Given Conditions
method_steps: Read the problem to identify the given conditions, which typically relate two or more terms of the AP or their properties.
For each condition, use the formula an = a + (n - 1)d to express the condition as a linear equation involving 'a' (first term) and 'd' (common difference).
This will result in a system of two (or more) linear equations with 'a' and 'd' as variables.
Solve the system of linear equations for 'a' and 'd' using an appropriate method (e.g., substitution, elimination).
Once 'a' and 'd' are determined, use these values to answer any further questions, such as constructing the AP or finding other terms.
isomorphic_variables: relationships_between_terms (e.g., sum, difference, ratio of terms)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly translating word problems or given conditions into algebraic equations (e.g., using n instead of n-1 in the formula, or confusing term values with term indices).
Making algebraic errors when solving the system of linear equations for 'a' and 'd'.
Hesitating to accept a negative or fractional value for 'd' if the calculation yields one.

nodes.name: Identify First Term and Common Difference from a Given AP
method_steps: Identify the first term 'a' directly from the sequence.
Calculate the difference between the second term and the first term to find 'd'.
Verify 'd' by calculating the difference between the third term and the second term.
isomorphic_variables: numerical values in the AP (integers, fractions, decimals, algebraic terms)
number of terms provided in the AP

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying 'a' (e.g., picking the second term instead of the first, or a simple reading error).
Subtracting terms in the wrong order (e.g., a1 - a2 instead of a2 - a1) or making arithmetic errors, especially with negative numbers or fractions.

nodes.name: Determine if a Sequence is an AP and Find Common Difference/Next Terms
method_steps: Calculate the difference between the second term and the first term (d1 = a2 - a1).
Calculate the difference between the third term and the second term (d2 = a3 - a2).
Compare d1 and d2. If they are not equal, the sequence is not an AP; state this conclusion.
If d1 = d2, continue calculating differences for more terms (d3 = a4 - a3, etc.) to confirm consistency.
If all consecutive differences are equal, the sequence is an AP, and this common difference is 'd'.
If it is an AP, calculate and write down the next term(s) by adding 'd' to the last known term.
isomorphic_variables: numerical values in the sequence (integers, fractions, decimals, algebraic terms)
number of terms provided in the sequence
number of subsequent terms to find

trap_steps.trap: Making arithmetic errors when calculating differences, especially with negative numbers, fractions, or decimals.
Concluding that a sequence is an AP after only calculating one difference, without checking consistency across all given terms.

nodes.name: Find a Specific Term or Related Property Using the nth Term Formula
method_steps: Identify or derive the first term 'a' and the common difference 'd' of the AP from the problem statement.
Identify the specific term number 'n' to find, or the target term value 'an', or other unknown variable required by the question.
Write down the general formula for the nth term of an AP: an = a + (n-1)d.
Substitute the known values (a, d, n, or an) into the formula.
Solve the resulting algebraic equation for the unknown variable.
If solving for 'n', ensure the result is a positive integer; if not, the term does not exist in the AP.
isomorphic_variables: relationships between terms (e.g., one term is X more than another)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying or deriving 'a' or 'd' from partially provided information (e.g., two non-consecutive terms).
Confusing 'n' (the position of the term) with 'an' (the value of the term at that position).
Algebraic errors when substituting values or solving the equation for the unknown variable.

nodes.name: Formulate an AP from a Real-World Scenario and Analyze It
method_steps: Read and understand the problem scenario to identify quantities that change sequentially.
List the first few terms (at least three) of the sequence formed by these quantities based on the problem description.
Check if this sequence is an Arithmetic Progression by calculating consecutive differences.
If it is an AP, clearly identify the first term 'a' and the common difference 'd'.
Apply the appropriate AP formula (e.g., `an = a + (n-1)d`) or properties to answer the specific question asked in the problem context.
State the final answer with appropriate units and in the context of the word problem.
isomorphic_variables: specific numerical values in the scenario (e.g., initial fare, interest rate, number of trees)
the context of the problem (e.g., taxi fare, simple interest, planting trees, construction steps, salaries)
the question being asked (e.g., find a term, find a total, check if it forms an AP)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly extracting the terms or initial values from the word problem, leading to an incorrect sequence or first term 'a'.
Incorrectly determining if the sequence forms an AP (e.g., miscalculating differences or not checking enough terms).
Misinterpreting what the problem asks for and applying an incorrect AP formula or property.

nodes.name: Identify an Arithmetic Progression and its Common Difference
method_steps: List the terms of the given sequence.
Calculate the difference between the second and first terms (a2 - a1).
Calculate the difference between the third and second terms (a3 - a2).
Compare the differences: if they are equal, the sequence is an Arithmetic Progression (AP).
The common difference 'd' is this constant value, and the first term 'a' is the first number in the sequence.
If asked, find subsequent terms by adding 'd' to the last known term.
isomorphic_variables: sequence_numbers (values, e.g., integers, fractions, algebraic terms)
context: simple_list -> word_problem (e.g., simple interest, salaries)

trap_steps.trap: Subtracting terms in the wrong order (e.g., a1 - a2 instead of a2 - a1), leading to an incorrect sign for 'd'.
Incorrectly concluding it's an AP after checking only one difference, or failing to verify all differences are constant.

nodes.name: Calculate a Specific Nth Term of an AP
method_steps: Identify the first term 'a' and the common difference 'd' of the AP.
Identify the position 'n' of the term to be found.
Substitute the values of 'a', 'd', and 'n' into the formula a_n = a + (n-1)d.
Perform the arithmetic operations to calculate the value of a_n.

trap_steps.trap: Using 'n' instead of '(n-1)' in the formula, leading to an incorrect value of the term.
Arithmetic errors in multiplication or addition/subtraction, especially with negative numbers or fractions.

nodes.name: Determine Term Position ('n') or Unknown AP Parameters ('a', 'd')
method_steps: Identify the known values: first term 'a', common difference 'd', the value of the nth term 'a_n', or relations between terms.
Write down the formula a_n = a + (n-1)d.
Substitute all known values into the formula.
Rearrange the equation and solve for the unknown variable (e.g., 'n', 'a', or 'd').
If 'n' is found, verify it is a positive integer. If it's not, the term does not exist in the AP.
For problems involving a term from the end: first calculate the total number of terms (N) in the AP. Then, the 'k'th term from the end is equivalent to the (N - k + 1)th term from the beginning.
For problems involving relations between terms (e.g., a_m and a_k): set up a system of linear equations using the a_n formula for each given term and solve for 'a' and 'd'.

trap_steps.trap: Algebraic errors when rearranging the equation to solve for the unknown variable, especially with negative numbers or distributing the common difference.
Not checking if 'n' is a positive integer, leading to accepting non-valid term positions (e.g., fractions or negative numbers).
Incorrectly converting 'kth term from the end' to 'nth term from the beginning' (e.g., using N-k instead of N-k+1).

nodes.name: Calculate Sum of an AP (S_n) Directly
method_steps: Identify the first term (a), common difference (d), and number of terms (n), or the first term (a), last term (l), and number of terms (n).
Choose the appropriate sum formula: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d] or S_n = (n/2)(a + l).
Substitute the identified values into the chosen formula.
Perform the arithmetic operations to find the sum (S_n).
isomorphic_variables: context (e.g., money saved, total distance, number of items)

trap_steps.trap: Forgetting the n/2 factor in the sum formula.
Making arithmetic errors during calculation.

nodes.name: Find Number of Terms (n) from Sum of AP (S_n)
method_steps: Identify the given values: first term (a), common difference (d), and the sum of n terms (S_n). (Alternatively, first term (a), last term (l), and S_n).
Write down the appropriate sum formula: S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d] or S_n = (n/2)(a + l).
Substitute the known values into the formula.
Simplify the equation, which typically leads to a quadratic equation in terms of n.
Solve the quadratic equation for n (e.g., using factorization or the quadratic formula).
Check the solutions for n: n must be a positive integer. Discard any non-positive or non-integer solutions.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up or simplifying the quadratic equation.
Making arithmetic errors or errors in applying the quadratic formula.
Not recognizing that 'n' must be a positive integer.

nodes.name: Solve for AP Parameters or Combined Problems (a, d, a_n, l)
method_steps: Read the problem carefully and identify all given information (e.g., a, d, n, l, a_n, S_n, or relationships between terms).
Translate word problems into mathematical expressions or equations involving a, d, n, l, a_n, S_n.
Determine which formulas (a_n = a + (n-1)d, S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d], S_n = (n/2)(a + l)) are needed to find the unknowns.
Set up a system of equations if multiple unknowns (e.g., a, d, n) need to be found.
Solve the system of equations or individual equations for the required parameters.
If the problem asks for S_n or a_n, calculate it using the values found.
Check if the solution makes sense in the context of the problem.
isomorphic_variables: context (e.g., production, prize money, tree planting, spiral length)

trap_steps.trap: Confusing a_n (the nth term) with S_n (the sum up to nth term).
Incorrectly setting up equations from word problems or given relationships.
Using the wrong formula (e.g., a_n when S_n is needed, or vice versa).
Errors in solving simultaneous equations or complex algebraic expressions.

nodes.name: Real-world problem: Find a specific term in an AP
method_steps: Read the problem carefully to understand the real-world scenario and identify the quantities that form an Arithmetic Progression.
Determine the first term (a) and the common difference (d) from the problem description, by analyzing the initial value and the constant rate of change.
Identify the specific term number (n) for which the value needs to be found, ensuring correct interpretation of 'nth' vs 'after n' units.
Apply the formula for the nth term of an AP: an = a + (n-1)d.
Calculate the value of 'an' and state the answer clearly in the context of the problem.
isomorphic_variables: numerical values for a, d, n

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying the first term 'a' or common difference 'd' from the word problem, especially if the progression starts indirectly or a 'zero-th' term is involved.
Misinterpreting the term number 'n', e.g., using 'n' for the 'nth' term when the problem asks for a value after 'n' changes (e.g., 'after 5 years' meaning the 6th term).
Confusing the nth term formula with the sum of n terms formula.
Making arithmetic errors during the calculation of the nth term.

nodes.name: Real-world problem: Find the sum of N terms of an AP
method_steps: Read the problem carefully to understand the real-world scenario and identify the quantities that form an Arithmetic Progression whose total sum is required.
Determine the first term (a), common difference (d), and the total number of terms (n) from the problem description.

Choose the appropriate sum formula: use Sn = n/2 * (a + l) if the last term (l) is directly given or easily found, otherwise use Sn = n/2 * [2a + (n-1)d]. If 'n' is unknown, set up the equation with the given sum and solve for 'n'.
Apply the chosen formula to calculate the sum 'Sn'. This may involve solving a quadratic equation for 'n' if 'n' was unknown.
State the total value in the context of the problem, ensuring units and interpretation are correct.
isomorphic_variables: context: trees planted->logs stacked->distances run->volumes accumulated
numerical values for a, d, n

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying the first term 'a', common difference 'd', or the total number of terms 'n' from the word problem, especially in cumulative scenarios.
Confusing the sum of n terms formula with the nth term formula, or selecting the wrong version of the sum formula (e.g., using 'l' incorrectly when 'l' isn't known).
Making arithmetic or algebraic errors while applying the formula, especially when solving quadratic equations for 'n' and handling multiple solutions or extraneous roots.

nodes.name: Identifying Basic Properties and Conditions of Similar Figures
method_steps: Read the statement or question carefully to identify the figures and the property being questioned (similarity or congruence).
Recall the precise definitions and conditions for similarity and congruence for the specific geometric figures (e.g., circles, squares, polygons).
Distinguish between similarity (same shape, different size possible) and congruence (same shape, same size).
Consider all conditions required for similarity of polygons (corresponding angles equal AND corresponding sides proportional).
Select the option or provide the answer that correctly applies the definitions and conditions.

trap_steps.trap: Confusing the definitions of similarity and congruence, assuming they are interchangeable or that one implies the other in all cases.
Assuming that for polygons, only one condition (either equal corresponding angles OR proportional corresponding sides) is sufficient for similarity.

nodes.name: Calculate missing segment lengths using BPT
method_steps: Identify the triangle and the line parallel to one of its sides.
Identify the corresponding segments formed on the other two sides.
Set up the proportion using the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT): AD/DB = AE/EC (or variations like AD/AB = AE/AC).
Substitute the given numerical values into the proportion.
Solve the equation for the unknown segment length.
isomorphic_variables: context (e.g., triangle within a larger figure)

trap_steps.trap: Applying BPT when the line is not given as parallel to a side.
Incorrectly setting up the ratio of segments (e.g., AD/AB = AE/EC instead of AD/DB = AE/EC).

nodes.name: Verify parallelism using Converse of BPT
method_steps: Identify the triangle and the line segment within it whose parallelism needs to be checked.
Identify the segments formed by this line on the two sides of the triangle.
Calculate the ratio of the segments on one side (e.g., AD/DB).
Calculate the ratio of the segments on the other side (e.g., AE/EC).
Compare the two ratios. If they are equal, the line is parallel to the third side by the Converse of BPT.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the ratio of segments (e.g., PE/EQ = PF/PR instead of PE/EQ = PF/FR).

nodes.name: Multi-step geometric proofs using BPT and/or its converse
method_steps: Analyze the given figure and statements to understand what needs to be proven.
Identify relevant triangles and parallel lines (or potential parallel lines) where BPT or its converse can be applied.
Apply BPT to derive proportional relationships from given parallel lines.
Apply Converse of BPT to prove lines are parallel if segment ratios are established.

Combine derived proportional relationships or parallel statements with other geometric properties (e.g., common sides, transitivity of parallelism, properties of specific quadrilaterals) to reach intermediate conclusions.
State the final conclusion clearly, citing all theorems and logical steps used.
isomorphic_variables: type of figure (e.g., trapezium, general triangle)
specific properties to prove (e.g., EF || QR, AD/ED = AE/FC)
auxiliary constructions (e.g., drawing a diagonal in a trapezium)

trap_steps.trap: Applying BPT or its converse incorrectly (e.g., not identifying parallel lines or unequal ratios).
Incorrectly setting up the ratio of segments within a BPT application.
Failing to connect different parts of the proof or misapplying other geometric theorems.

nodes.name: Verify Parallelism using Segment Ratios (Direct Converse of BPT)
method_steps: Identify the triangle and the line segment intersecting two of its sides.
Identify the two pairs of segments formed on the intersected sides.
Calculate the ratio of the segments on the first side (e.g., AD/DB).
Calculate the ratio of the segments on the second side (e.g., AE/EC).
Compare the two calculated ratios.
If the ratios are equal, conclude that the line is parallel to the third side (Converse of BPT); otherwise, conclude it is not parallel.
isomorphic_variables: triangle vertices (e.g., P, Q, R or A, B, C)
contextual figure (e.g., simple triangle, or a larger figure where a triangle is isolated for analysis)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly forming the ratio of segments on a side (e.g., using A/B = C/D instead of A/B = X/Y, or mixing whole side with segment).
Incorrectly forming the ratio of segments on the other side.
Misinterpreting the equality or inequality of the calculated ratios.
Confusing the Converse of BPT with the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) itself, attempting to use BPT to prove parallelism.

nodes.name: Prove Parallelism via Intermediate Ratios (Chained BPT & Converse BPT)
method_steps: Analyze the given figure and identify triangles where the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) can be applied based on given parallel lines.
Apply BPT in the first relevant triangle(s) to establish a ratio of segments (e.g., OA/AP = OB/BQ).
Apply BPT in a second relevant triangle(s) to establish another ratio, linking to the previous ratio via a common segment or point (e.g., OA/AP = OC/CR).
Use transitivity or substitution to equate the derived ratios (e.g., conclude OB/BQ = OC/CR).
Identify the target triangle and the line segment within it for which parallelism needs to be proven.
Apply the Converse of BPT to the target triangle using the equated ratios to conclude parallelism (e.g., BC || QR).
isomorphic_variables: points on lines (e.g., A, B, C, P, Q, R, O, D, E, F, G)
figure configuration (e.g., triangles sharing a common vertex, embedded triangles)
symbolic labels instead of numerical values for lengths

trap_steps.trap: Failure to correctly identify the constituent triangles or the necessary auxiliary constructions (if any) required to apply BPT.
Incorrect application of BPT, setting up incorrect ratios based on given parallel lines.
Incorrect application of BPT in the second triangle or failure to identify ratios that link to the first set.
Algebraic errors in equating or simplifying the derived ratios.
Confusing the Converse of BPT with BPT, attempting to use BPT to prove parallelism from the derived ratios.

nodes.name: Proving Triangle Similarity using AA, SSS, or SAS Criteria
method_steps: Identify the two triangles that need to be proven similar.
Carefully identify and list corresponding vertices based on potential angle/side relationships.
Examine the given information (e.g., equal angles, proportional side lengths, parallel lines, properties of geometric figures like altitudes, medians, or congruency).
Identify pairs of equal corresponding angles or proportional corresponding sides from the given information or derived properties.
Determine which similarity criterion (AA, SSS, or SAS) can be applied based on the identified relationships.
State the chosen criterion and conclude that the triangles are similar, explicitly writing the similarity statement with correctly matched corresponding vertices (e.g., Δ ABC ~ Δ PQR).
isomorphic_variables: context: specific geometric figures (trapezium, parallelogram, altitudes, medians)
type of similarity criterion (AA, SSS, SAS)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly matching corresponding vertices, leading to incorrect comparisons of angles or sides.
Attempting to apply an incomplete or incorrect similarity criterion (e.g., using Angle-Side-Side, or not ensuring the angle is included in SAS).

nodes.name: Applying Triangle Similarity Properties to find Unknowns (Angles or Side Ratios)
method_steps: Identify the similar triangles (either given as similar or proven in a prior step).
List the corresponding vertices correctly between the similar triangles.
Based on the unknown, either formulate ratios of corresponding sides for lengths/proportions or equate corresponding angles for angle measures.
Set up algebraic equations using the established proportions or angle equalities.
Solve the equations to find the unknown values (e.g., side lengths, angles, or prove a specific ratio).
Verify the reasonableness of the calculated values in the context of the problem.
isomorphic_variables: type of unknown (angle, side length, ratio, or specific proportion to prove)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly matching corresponding vertices when setting up ratios or angle equalities, leading to incorrect calculations.
Setting up incorrect ratios of sides (e.g., mixing non-corresponding sides or inverting ratios inconsistently).

nodes.name: Distinguishing Similarity Criteria for Triangles vs. General Polygons
method_steps: Recall the general definition of similar polygons: corresponding angles are equal AND corresponding sides are proportional.
Understand that for general polygons, both of these conditions must be met simultaneously for similarity.
Recall that for triangles, fewer specific criteria (AA, SSS, or SAS) are sufficient to prove similarity, meaning one or two conditions implicitly satisfy the others.
Apply the appropriate set of conditions or criteria based on whether the figures are general polygons or specifically triangles to determine similarity.
isomorphic_variables: types of polygons (circles, squares, equilateral triangles, quadrilaterals)
specific examples of conditions (equal angles, proportional sides)

trap_steps.trap: Applying the stricter 'both conditions' rule from general polygons unnecessarily to triangles, instead of using simpler criteria like AA, SSS, or SAS.

nodes.name: Prove Triangle Similarity (AAA/AA Criterion)
method_steps: Identify the two triangles for which similarity needs to be proven.
Examine the given information (diagram, text) for parallel lines, common vertices, perpendicular lines, etc.

Identify pairs of corresponding angles that are equal using geometric theorems (e.g., alternate interior angles, corresponding angles, vertically opposite angles, common angles, angles in a right triangle).
If two pairs of corresponding angles are proven equal, conclude that the third pair must also be equal (Angle Sum Property).
State that the two triangles are similar by the AAA (or AA) similarity criterion, ensuring correct correspondence of vertices.
isomorphic_variables: geometric configuration (e.g., parallel lines, intersecting lines, shared vertex)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying corresponding angles or applying angle theorems (e.g., confusing alternate interior with corresponding angles).
Stating similarity based on insufficient evidence (e.g., only one pair of equal angles) or incorrectly matching corresponding vertices.

nodes.name: Apply Similarity (AAA/AA) to Find Unknown Lengths/Proportions
method_steps: Identify the two triangles involved and any unknown lengths or values to be found.
Prove or establish that the two triangles are similar using an appropriate criterion (e.g., AA from perpendiculars and common angle, or using parallel lines).
Write down the proportionality of corresponding sides based on the similarity (e.g., AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF).
Substitute known values into the proportion, forming an equation.
Solve the resulting equation(s) to find the unknown length(s) or prove the required proportion.
isomorphic_variables: context (e.g., lamp-post/shadow, ladder, building, general geometry)
type of unknown (x, y, specific ratio)

trap_steps.trap: Assuming similarity without proper proof, or incorrectly identifying conditions for similarity.
Incorrectly identifying corresponding sides when setting up proportions after similarity is established.
Algebraic errors when setting up or solving the proportional equation.

nodes.name: Understand Conditions for Polygon Similarity
method_steps: Recall the definition of similar polygons (for polygons in general, not just triangles).
Examine the given polygons to determine if their corresponding angles are equal.
Examine the given polygons to determine if their corresponding sides are proportional.
Conclude if the polygons are similar based on both conditions (equal angles AND proportional sides) being met.

trap_steps.trap: Assuming polygons are similar if only angles are equal, or only sides are proportional (this is true for triangles with AA/SSS/SAS, but not for general polygons like quadrilaterals).

nodes.name: Proving Triangle Similarity and Deriving Ratios in Geometric Figures
method_steps: Identify the two triangles for which similarity needs to be proven.
Analyze the given geometric figure and information to find properties that imply equal angles (e.g., parallel lines, perpendicular lines, properties of specific shapes like isosceles triangles).

Identify pairs of equal angles: look for vertically opposite angles, alternate interior angles, corresponding angles, common angles, or angles from shape properties (e.g., base angles of isosceles triangle, right angles).
Select two distinct pairs of corresponding angles that are proven to be equal.
Conclude that the two triangles are similar by the AA (Angle-Angle) similarity criterion.
If required, use the property of similar triangles to set up ratios of corresponding sides or deduce equality of other angles.
Manipulate the ratios to prove the desired relationship (if applicable).
isomorphic_variables: types of geometric shapes (isosceles triangle, trapezium)

trap_steps.trap: Student attempts to find side ratios or an included angle to apply SAS/SSS instead of focusing on angles for AA.
Students might overlook hidden angle relationships (e.g., alternate interior angles with parallel lines, common angles).
Student identifies two pairs of equal angles but hesitates to conclude similarity, thinking a third pair is needed.
Students might set up incorrect ratios of sides after proving similarity, confusing corresponding sides.

nodes.name: Real-World Application of AA Similarity for Measurement
method_steps: Read the problem carefully and visualize the physical situation.
Draw a clear diagram representing the situation, labeling all given lengths and unknowns.
Identify two triangles within the diagram that represent the situation and can be proven similar.
Identify the first pair of equal angles, typically right angles (e.g., objects perpendicular to the ground).
Identify the second pair of equal angles, often a common angle (e.g., angle of elevation from a single point, angle of intersection).
Conclude that the two triangles are similar by the AA (Angle-Angle) similarity criterion.
Set up an equation using the proportionality of corresponding sides of the similar triangles.
Solve the equation for the unknown length or quantity.
isomorphic_variables: types of objects (lamp-post, person, tree, building)
context of measurement (shadow length, distance, height)

trap_steps.trap: Student attempts to establish side proportionality for SAS/SSS instead of identifying angles for AA, misinterpreting the problem's implicit use of AA, or struggles to correctly identify the two relevant triangles from the word problem or draw an inaccurate diagram.
Students might fail to identify the common angle or another source for the second pair of equal angles.
Student identifies two pairs of equal angles but hesitates to conclude similarity, thinking a third pair is needed.
Students might incorrectly match corresponding sides when setting up the proportion.

nodes.name: Direct SSS Similarity Verification
method_steps: Identify the corresponding sides of the two triangles based on their lengths or given correspondence.
Calculate the ratios of the lengths of the identified corresponding sides.
Check if all three calculated ratios are equal. Ensure the ratios are simplified correctly.
If all three ratios are equal, state that the triangles are similar by the SSS (Side-Side-Side) similarity criterion.
Use the established similarity to deduce other properties, such as the equality of corresponding angles or proportionality of other segments.
isomorphic_variables: context: finding angle/side after proving similarity

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly matching corresponding sides, especially when triangles are rotated or reflected.
Miscalculating side ratios or failing to check if all three ratios are equal.
Confusing the SSS similarity criterion (proportional sides) with the SSS congruence criterion (equal sides).

nodes.name: SSS Similarity Proof with Proportional Medians
method_steps: Understand the given conditions: two sides and a median of one triangle are proportional to the corresponding elements of another triangle.
Construct auxiliary lines (e.g., extend medians) to create smaller triangles or parallelograms that can aid in proving proportionality or angle equality.
Use the properties of medians and the given proportionality to prove the similarity (often by SSS, SAS, or AA) of these newly formed smaller triangles.
From the similarity of the smaller triangles, deduce the proportionality of the third pair of corresponding sides of the main triangles, or the equality of corresponding angles.
Apply the SSS (Side-Side-Side) similarity criterion to conclude that the main triangles are similar.

trap_steps.trap: Difficulty in identifying or correctly constructing appropriate auxiliary lines to facilitate the proof.
Incorrectly applying properties of medians or setting up ratios for the smaller triangles.
Confusing SSS similarity with SSS congruence when drawing the final conclusion.

nodes.name: Proving Triangle Similarity using Direct SAS Criterion
method_steps: Identify the two triangles for which similarity needs to be proven.
Identify one pair of equal angles between the two triangles (e.g., common angle, vertically opposite angles, or explicitly given equal angles).
Identify the pair of sides that *include* this equal angle in each triangle.

Establish that the ratio of corresponding sides including the identified equal angle is proportional (i.e., `side1_A / side1_B = side2_A / side2_B`). This may involve algebraic manipulation from given products or substitution based on other geometric properties (like congruence or isosceles triangle properties).
Conclude that the two triangles are similar by the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity criterion.
Optionally, use the established similarity to deduce other properties (e.g., proportional sides, equal corresponding angles).
isomorphic_variables: specific numerical values of side lengths or ratios
type of equal angle (e.g., common, vertically opposite, alternate interior)

trap_steps.trap: Attempts to establish proportionality using sides that do not include the identified equal angle, or using non-corresponding sides.
Confuses SAS similarity with SAS congruence, expecting sides to be equal rather than proportional.

nodes.name: Proving Triangle Similarity with Proportional Medians (using SAS as final step)
method_steps: Identify the main triangles (e.g., ΔABC and ΔPQR) whose similarity needs to be proven.
Identify the given proportionality of corresponding sides and medians (e.g., AB/PQ = BC/QR = AD/PM).
Recall that a median bisects the opposite side, so express the halves of the proportional sides in terms of the median endpoints (e.g., BD = BC/2 and QM = QR/2).
Form smaller triangles involving the medians and half-sides (e.g., ΔABD and ΔPQM).
Use the given proportionality to show similarity of these smaller triangles (e.g., AB/PQ = AD/PM = BD/QM implies ΔABD ~ ΔPQM by SSS similarity criterion).
From the similarity of the smaller triangles, deduce that the included angles of the main triangles are equal (e.g., corresponding angles ∠B = ∠Q).

Apply the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity criterion to the main triangles, using the initially given proportional sides (e.g., AB/PQ = BC/QR) and the newly proven equal included angle (e.g., ∠B = ∠Q).
Conclude that the main triangles are similar.
isomorphic_variables: specific numerical values of side lengths or ratios

trap_steps.trap: Fails to correctly identify or apply the similarity criterion (e.g., SSS) to the smaller triangles, leading to an incorrect deduction of equal angles.
Confuses SAS similarity with SAS congruence, expecting sides to be equal rather than proportional in the final step.

nodes.name: Calculate Distance(s) and Determine Basic Geometric Properties
method_steps: Identify the coordinates of the points for which distance is to be calculated (e.g., P(x1, y1), Q(x2, y2)).
Calculate the difference in x-coordinates (x2 - x1) and y-coordinates (y2 - y1).
Substitute these differences into the distance formula: d = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²].
Square both differences.
Add the squared differences.
Take the square root of the sum to find the distance.
If multiple distances are required, repeat steps 1-6 for each pair of points.
Apply the relevant geometric condition (e.g., check AB+BC=AC for collinearity, or Pythagorean theorem for a right triangle).
isomorphic_variables: specific geometric property (collinearity, right triangle, isosceles triangle, equilateral triangle)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly identifying or transcribing coordinates for the points.
Confusing the x-coordinate difference with the y-coordinate difference or vice-versa.
Forgetting to take the square root at the end of the calculation.

nodes.name: Classify a Polygon using Distance Formula
method_steps: List all given vertices with their coordinates.
Identify all sides and diagonals whose lengths are needed for polygon classification.
For each required segment, identify its endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).
Calculate the differences (x2 - x1) and (y2 - y1).
Substitute these differences into the distance formula: d = √[ (x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)² ].
Perform the squaring, addition, and square root operations to find the length of the segment.
Repeat steps 3-6 for all identified sides and diagonals.
Compare the calculated lengths against the known geometric properties of the target polygon type (e.g., for a square: all sides equal, diagonals equal).
Conclude the classification based on the comparison.
isomorphic_variables: type of polygon (square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram)

trap_steps.trap: Not identifying all necessary sides and diagonals required to definitively classify the polygon.
Incorrectly identifying or transcribing coordinates for segment endpoints.
Confusing the x-coordinate difference with the y-coordinate difference or vice-versa.
Forgetting to take the square root at the end of the calculation for segment lengths.
Incorrectly recalling or applying the specific geometric properties for classifying the polygon.

nodes.name: Find an Equidistant Point on an Axis or Plane
method_steps: Represent the unknown equidistant point using variables based on its location (e.g., (x, 0) for x-axis, (0, y) for y-axis, or (x, y) for a general point).
Identify the two (or more) known points from which the unknown point is equidistant.
Set up an equation stating that the squared distance from the unknown point to the first known point is equal to the squared distance from the unknown point to the second known point (PA² = PB²).
Calculate the differences in x-coordinates and y-coordinates for both PA and PB.
Substitute these differences into the squared distance formula components: (x - xA)² + (y - yA)² = (x - xB)² + (y - yB)².
Expand and simplify the algebraic equation by squaring terms and combining like terms.
Solve the resulting linear or quadratic equation(s) for the unknown coordinate(s).
State the coordinates of the equidistant point.
isomorphic_variables: location of unknown point (x-axis, y-axis, general (x,y))

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly representing the unknown point based on its given location (e.g., using (x,y) instead of (0,y) for a point on the y-axis).
Confusing the x-coordinate difference with the y-coordinate difference or vice-versa for either distance calculation.
Errors in substituting coordinates into the distance formula components.
Algebraic errors during expansion and simplification (e.g., (a-b)^2, combining like terms).
Errors in solving the resulting linear or quadratic equation.

nodes.name: Determining Collinearity of Three Points using Distance Formula
method_steps: Identify the coordinates of the three given points, say A, B, and C.
Calculate the distance between each pair of points using the distance formula: AB, BC, and AC.
Identify the two smallest distances and the largest distance among the three calculated distances.
Check if the sum of the two smaller distances is exactly equal to the largest distance.
If the equality holds, conclude that the points are collinear.
Otherwise, conclude that the points are not collinear.
State the final conclusion clearly, providing a reason based on the distance comparison.
isomorphic_variables: point_labels (e.g., 'A, B, C', 'P, Q, R', 'Ashima, Bharti, Camella')
coordinates_numbers (the specific numerical values of the coordinates)
context (e.g., 'geometric points', 'people seated in a classroom')
question_wording (e.g., 'Do you think they are seated in a line?', 'Determine if the points are collinear')

trap_steps.trap: Algebraic errors (e.g., sign errors when subtracting coordinates, errors in squaring negative numbers, arithmetic errors in addition/subtraction under the square root) while calculating distances.
Misidentifying the two shorter distances or the longest distance, or not considering all three pairs of distances when selecting which ones to sum.

Performing the sum check using approximate decimal values which might lead to an incorrect conclusion if not exact (e.g., due to rounding errors). The check should ideally be done with exact square root values or high precision.
Drawing a conclusion about collinearity based solely on visual inspection of a graph or diagram without performing the necessary distance calculations.

nodes.name: Classify type of triangle given its vertices
method_steps: Assign coordinates to the three vertices (e.g., A, B, C).
Calculate the length of each side using the distance formula: AB, BC, and CA.

Compare the side lengths to determine primary classification (e.g., If all three are equal, it's an equilateral triangle; if two sides are equal, it's an isosceles triangle; if all three are different, it's a scalene triangle).
Check if the square of the longest side is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides (Pythagorean theorem). If true, it's a right-angled triangle.
Combine primary classification with the right-angle check (e.g., isosceles right-angled triangle) and state the type with reasoning.
isomorphic_variables: context: points vs locations on a map

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly applying the distance formula, leading to wrong side lengths.
Only checking for equality of sides and missing the Pythagorean check for a right angle.
Applying Pythagoras theorem incorrectly or not at all.

nodes.name: Classify type of quadrilateral given its vertices
method_steps: Assign coordinates to the four vertices (e.g., A, B, C, D) in order.
Calculate the length of all four sides (AB, BC, CD, DA) using the distance formula.
Calculate the length of both diagonals (AC, BD) using the distance formula.
Analyze side lengths: If all four sides are equal, it's a rhombus. If opposite sides are equal (AB=CD, BC=DA), it's a parallelogram.
Analyze diagonal lengths: If diagonals are equal (AC=BD), it indicates a rectangle (if it's a parallelogram) or a square (if it's a rhombus).
Combine results to determine the specific quadrilateral type (e.g., rhombus + equal diagonals = square; parallelogram + equal diagonals = rectangle).
State the type and provide reasoning based on the calculated lengths.
isomorphic_variables: specific type of quadrilateral to prove (square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly calculating one or more side lengths, leading to misclassification.
Forgetting to calculate diagonal lengths or miscalculating them, which are crucial for distinguishing between rhombuses/squares and parallelograms/rectangles.
Confusing the properties required to identify different quadrilaterals (e.g., only checking sides for a square without checking diagonals or angles).
Concluding 'no quadrilateral' prematurely without verifying all conditions.

nodes.name: Determine if three given points are collinear
method_steps: Assign coordinates to the three points (e.g., A, B, C).
Calculate the distance between all three pairs of points using the distance formula: AB, BC, and AC.
Identify the two smallest distances and the largest distance among the three calculated lengths.
Check if the sum of the two smaller distances is equal to the largest distance (i.e., d1 + d2 = d3).
If the sum is equal, the points are collinear; otherwise, they are not collinear.
isomorphic_variables: context: physical arrangement vs abstract points

trap_steps.trap: Miscalculating any of the three distances.
Incorrectly comparing the distances, e.g., adding any two distances instead of the two smallest, or comparing squares of distances instead of distances themselves.

nodes.name: Find unknown coordinate(s) satisfying a distance condition
method_steps: Identify the given points and the unknown coordinate(s). Assign a variable (e.g., x or y) to the unknown coordinate.
Formulate the distance condition as an algebraic equation using the distance formula (e.g., set two distances equal if points are equidistant, or set a distance equal to a given value).
Square both sides of the equation to eliminate the square root.
Simplify and solve the resulting algebraic equation (which may be linear or quadratic) for the unknown variable(s).
Substitute the found value(s) back into the coordinates to state the final point(s) or coordinate value(s).
isomorphic_variables: axis on which point lies (x-axis vs y-axis)
number of unknown coordinates (one vs two if a relationship is given)

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the distance formula or the equality condition based on the problem statement.
Errors in squaring binomials or expanding terms after squaring the distance formula.
Algebraic errors when solving the resulting equation (e.g., sign errors, incorrect factoring, or misapplication of the quadratic formula).
Missing one or more possible solutions, especially when solving quadratic equations.

nodes.name: Calculate Coordinates of Internal Division Point
method_steps: Identify the two endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) of the line segment.
Identify the given internal ratio m:n in which the point divides the segment.
Apply the section formula for the x-coordinate: x = (m*x2 + n*x1) / (m + n).
Apply the section formula for the y-coordinate: y = (m*y2 + n*y1) / (m + n).
State the coordinates of the division point (x, y).

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly applying the ratio to coordinates (e.g., m*x1 + n*x2 instead of m*x2 + n*x1)
Applying the ratio m:n to the y-coordinates in reverse order or incorrectly
Using external division formula (or negative ratio) when internal division is required

nodes.name: Determine Ratio of Internal Division
method_steps: Identify the two endpoints (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) and the division point (x, y).
Assume the ratio of division as k:1 (or m:n).
Apply the section formula for either the x-coordinate (x = (k*x2 + 1*x1) / (k + 1)) or the y-coordinate (y = (k*y2 + 1*y1) / (k + 1)).
Solve the chosen equation for k.
Verify the ratio using the other coordinate (optional but recommended).
State the ratio of division in the form k:1 or m:n.

trap_steps.trap: Incorrectly setting up the equation for k (e.g., swapping x1, x2 or misplacing k)
Algebraic error when solving for k
